summary: This document specifies fault management for Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL) Operations, Administration, and Maintenance. It follows the IEEE 802.1 Connectivity Fault Management framework and reuses parts of it.

eli5.summary: When a network path breaks, you need ways to check and find the problem. This describes the tests that let operators of this kind of network check on their links.

questions: how to detect faults in trill
how does trill path trace work
what is the trill alert flag
subtitle: The fault-finding tools for TRILL networks: loopback, path trace, multicast tree checks and continuity checks.

tldr.problem: TRILL spreads traffic over many equal-cost paths, so operators need ways to check connectivity and find faults on the same path a given data flow would take.
tldr.mechanism: OAM frames are marked with an Alert flag in the TRILL header and carry an IEEE 802.1 CFM message, with a copy of the flow's entropy so they follow the data path. The RFC reuses CFM Loopback and Continuity Check messages and adds Path Trace and Multi-destination Tree Verification.
tldr.outcome: Operators get a ping-like loopback, a traceroute-like path trace, multicast tree checks and per-flow continuity monitoring. The RFC updates RFC 6325 to add the Alert flag.

sections.title: Fault Management on CFM
sections.content:
This RFC specifies OAM (Operations, Administration, and Maintenance) fault management for TRILL. TRILL switches are also known as RBridges. The OAM messages follow the Connectivity Fault Management (CFM) framework from IEEE 802.1 and reuse its tools where possible. Extra messages and TLVs are defined for TRILL-specific needs or where different information is required.

TRILL OAM frames have six parts: Link Header, TRILL Header, Flow Entropy, OAM Ethertype, OAM Message Channel and Link Trailer. The general structure comes from RFC 7174, and TRILL performance monitoring is in RFC 7456. The document assumes the reader knows IEEE 802.1Q and ITU-T Y.1731.
sections.eli5: TRILL borrows an existing set of network test tools and adds a few new ones for its own needs.

sections.title: OAM Frame Format and the Alert Flag
sections.content:
TRILL picks one of several equal-cost paths per hop, so OAM messages must follow the same path as the data they stand for. To do that, the frame holds a Flow Entropy field, 96 bytes that start at the Inner.MacDA and are zero-padded on the right when shorter. The TRILL Header is 6 bytes when there is no extension. The OAM Ethertype is 0x8902, the one allocated for CFM.

TRILL as defined in RFC 6325 had no way to mark OAM frames, so this RFC updates it. It uses a reserved header bit next to the Version field as the Alert flag (A). RBridges MUST NOT use the A flag for forwarding decisions such as choosing an ECMP path or distribution tree. A frame with A set is only an OAM frame if the CFM Ethertype is at the expected spot; otherwise it MUST be silently discarded. OAM-capable RBridges MUST NOT send OAM frames to an RBridge that is not OAM capable, and non-capable intermediate RBridges forward A-flag frames unchanged.

Capability is announced with two flags in the TRILL-VER sub-TLV (RFC 7176): O for OAM capable and B for the backwards-compatible method of Appendix A. That older method, meant only as an interim solution, spots OAM frames by well-known values (the unicast and multicast MAC addresses 00-00-5E-90-01-00 and 01-00-5E-90-01-00) instead of the A flag.
sections.eli5: The test message wears a special sticker so routers know it is a test, but the sticker never changes which road it takes.

sections.title: Layering, Maintenance Points and Addressing
sections.content:
The TRILL OAM layer sits between the TRILL encapsulation layer and the RBridge layer. It picks out OAM frames needing local processing and either handles them or passes them to the CPU. The TRILL layer is responsible for preventing OAM packets from leaking out as native frames.

A Maintenance Association (MA) is a group of nodes and is identified by a 48-byte MAID used unchanged from IEEE 802.1Q. In TRILL a Maintenance End Point (MEP) is addressed by the egress RBridge nickname plus the Inner.VLAN or fine-grained label, rather than by a MAC address. A MEP-ID MUST be in the range 1 to 65535. Each MEP also keeps one or more Flow Entropy definitions for the flows it monitors.

Inside a MEP, a frame passes through MD-Level demultiplexers and then an OpCode demultiplexer. A frame at a lower level than the MEP is discarded, an equal level goes to the OpCode demultiplexer, and a higher level moves on or is forwarded as data. Unknown OpCodes are discarded. Maintenance Intermediate Points (MIPs) are used mainly for fault isolation, and the Path Trace message works like IP traceroute by expiring the Hop Count, so MIPs need not be addressed individually. On edge interfaces, MEPs MUST be configured to stop OAM packets leaking out of the TRILL campus.

The Base Mode (Appendix B) gives plug-and-play operation. All RBridges that support OAM MUST support it. It uses the MD-Level 3 and the Maintenance Domain Name string TrillBaseMode, and each RBridge creates a single UP MEP whose MEP-ID is its 2-octet nickname.
sections.eli5: Each router has a checkpoint that looks at test messages. Ones from a lower level are thrown away, ones for this level are handled, and others pass on through.

sections.title: The OAM Message Channel and TLVs
sections.content:
Every OAM message has one header and one or more TLVs. The header is the CFM header: MD-Level (3 bits), Version (5 bits), OpCode (8 bits), Flags (1 byte) and FirstTLVOffset (1 byte). The TLV format is also CFM's: a 1-octet Type, a 2-octet Length and a variable Value. TRILL reuses CFM types such as Sender ID (1), Interface Status (4), Reply Ingress (5) and Reply Egress (6), and adds types 64 to 74.

The TRILL OAM Application Identifier TLV (64) MUST be the first TLV, and an End TLV (0) MUST be last. It holds the OAM Version (currently zero), a Fragment-ID, a Return Code and Sub-code, and four flags: F (final reply), C (cross-connect error, label mismatch), O (out-of-band response requested) and I (in-band response requested). With both O and I clear the message is in silent mode and no reply is wanted.

Other TLVs include the Out-of-Band Reply Address (IPv4, IPv6 or a TRILL nickname), the Diagnostic Label (a VLAN or a 24-bit fine-grained label), the Original Data Payload (the original TRILL header and Flow Entropy), the RBridge Scope, the Previous RBridge Nickname, the Next-Hop RBridge List, the Multicast Receiver Port Count, the Flow Identifier, the Reflector Entropy and an Authentication TLV.
sections.eli5: Every test message has a fixed front page, then a stack of labeled notes. The first note must always say what kind of test it is.

sections.title: Loopback and Path Trace
sections.content:
The Loopback Message is the CFM one (OpCode 3, reply OpCode 2) and carries a 32-bit Loopback Transaction Identifier that responders echo unchanged. The originator names a destination RBridge, builds the Flow Entropy, sets a Hop Count and sends. Intermediate RBridges forward it as ordinary data. The destination sends a reply with Return Code 1 and Sub-code 0 (valid response), either in-band back to the originator's nickname or out-of-band through IP. The originator may retransmit, incrementing the Session ID each time.

The Path Trace Message (OpCode 65, reply 64) has the same format as Loopback, and is used mainly for fault isolation or plotting a path. It is first sent with Hop Count 1. An intermediate RBridge whose Hop Count expires answers with Sub-code 2 (Intermediate RBridge) and includes TLVs such as the previous RBridge nickname, the interfaces and the next-hop list (repeated for each ECMP choice). The originator records this and resends with the Hop Count increased by 1, continuing until the destination answers, the process times out or a configured maximum Hop Count is reached. The RFC uses this instead of CFM Link Trace because multicast and unicast paths are not congruent in TRILL.
sections.eli5: Loopback is like shouting across the field and hearing an echo. Path trace is like walking one step further each time and asking whoever you meet to say hello.

sections.title: Multi-destination Tree Verification
sections.content:
The Multi-destination Tree Verification Message (MTVM, OpCode 67, reply 66) checks that a distribution tree and its pruning work, and can plot a multicast tree. It has the same format as Loopback. MTVM frames are copied to the CPU of every RBridge on the tree, so the originator names the responders in an RBridge Scope TLV. Only listed RBridges answer and others silently discard it. Without a Scope TLV, every RBridge answers.

The user must be able to choose at least the distribution tree, the destination multicast MAC address and the VLAN or fine-grained label. Replies carry the Previous RBridge Nickname, Reply Ingress, Interface Status, Next-Hop RBridge List, Sender ID and Multicast Receiver Port Count TLVs. Because implementations MAY rate-limit CPU-bound multicast traffic, some messages may be dropped. Retransmissions SHOULD narrow the scope to RBridges that have not responded.
sections.eli5: To check a group chat reaches everyone, you can ask a chosen list of friends to reply. Anyone not on the list stays quiet.

sections.title: Continuity Checks and Fragmented Replies
sections.content:
Continuity Check Messages (CCMs) are one-way heartbeats with no reply. TRILL has several possible paths between two MEPs, so each MEP monitors per-flow connectivity using the Flow Entropy list in its MA. A MEP sends four CCMs per flow, each with a unique sequence number and a Flow Identifier TLV, then moves to the next flow. CCM timeout in 802.1Q is three missed intervals.

When a MEP detects a timeout from a remote MEP, it sets the Remote Defect Indication (RDI) flag in its next CCM. It also logs and sends an SNMP notification with the remote MEP, the flow identifier and the sequence number of the last CCM received. When CCMs resume it sends a notification with the first valid flow identifier and sequence number. This lets an operator work out which flow was at fault without tracking every flow's state.

Replies may be split into fragments. They share one Session ID, the Fragment-ID rises with each fragment and the Final flag is set only on the last. Fragments after the final one MUST be discarded, as MUST incomplete messages. If the number of fragments exceeds the 255 maximum, the reply uses Return Code 1 and Sub-code 1 (fragment limit exceeded).
sections.eli5: Continuity checks are like two friends flashing a light to each other every few seconds. If the light stops, they note which route the last flash used.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Forged OAM packets could cause false failure reports, hide real failures or be used for denial of service. The out-of-band reply address can also be supplied by the sender. The optional Authentication TLV is nearly the same as the IS-IS one and relies on IS-IS keying. The RFC notes that there is no standardized automated IS-IS key management. Authentication is ineffective unless verified, and sender with the keys can still forge messages. Implementations MUST rate-limit OAM messages, though aggressive limits may cause false errors in CCM and loopback monitoring.

Every message type has a sequence or transaction identifier that can help detect replay. The MD-Level is buried deep in the message, so frames that should be dropped may leak into a domain with a different level. The RFC argues this does not cause functional loss, since receivers validate the level. It also notes that a TRILL campus is generally managed by one operator.
sections.eli5: Anyone could fake a test message, so the network can sign them and slow down floods. Signing needs shared secret keys, and those must be set up carefully.
